boards.prompt: Write the polar decomposition F = RU. How do you actually compute U and R, and what does each one mean physically? Now give me the left version.
points: U = √C, the symmetric positive definite right stretch tensor, with C = FᵀF
Eigenvalues of U are the principal stretches, its eigenvectors are principal directions in the reference configuration
R = FU⁻¹ is a proper orthogonal rotation, RᵀR = I and det R = 1
Left form F = VR with V = √B = RURᵀ and B = FFᵀ
V has the same principal stretches, with principal directions rotated by R into the current configuration

boards.prompt: Define the velocity gradient and split it into symmetric and skew parts. Which part stretches material, and how is it connected to the rate of Green strain?
points: L = ∂v/∂x = ḞF⁻¹
D = ½(L + Lᵀ) is the rate of deformation, the stretching rate
W = ½(L − Lᵀ) is the spin, a rigid rotation rate
Ė = FᵀDF, the pull back of D to the reference configuration
J̇ = J tr D = J div v

boards.prompt: Take u₁ = k x₂, u₂ = 0 with k small. Split the displacement gradient into strain and rotation. What does each part look like on the board?
points: ∇u = ε + ω, with ε the symmetric part and ω the skew part
ε₁₂ = ε₂₁ = k/2 and every other strain component is zero
Engineering shear strain γ₁₂ = 2ε₁₂ = k
ω₁₂ = −ω₂₁ = k/2, a rigid rotation of size k/2
Simple shear equals pure shear plus a rigid rotation

boards.prompt: Split F into a volume change and a distortion. Why do people do this for rubber and for metal plasticity?
points: J = det F is the volume ratio
F̄ = J^(−1/3) F has det F̄ = 1, the isochoric part
F = (J^(1/3) I) F̄, a uniform dilatation times a distortion
Rubber and plastic flow are nearly volume preserving, so the bulk response goes on J and the shear response on C̄

boards.prompt: Derive Cauchy's formula from a tetrahedron. What happens to the body force and the inertia as the tetrahedron shrinks?
points: Tetrahedron with three faces normal to the axes and an inclined face with normal n and area dA
Face areas are dA_i = n_i dA
Body force and inertia scale with the volume, h dA, and drop out as h → 0
Force balance gives t = σn, t_i = σ_ij n_j using the symmetry of σ
Traction is linear in n, so the stress tensor fixes the traction on every plane through the point

boards.prompt: Find the normal and shear traction on the octahedral plane. Then connect the octahedral shear to von Mises.
points: In principal axes the octahedral normal is n = (1, 1, 1)/√3
σ_oct = (σ₁ + σ₂ + σ₃)/3, the mean stress
τ_oct = ⅓√((σ₁ − σ₂)² + (σ₂ − σ₃)² + (σ₃ − σ₁)²)
σ_vM = (3/√2) τ_oct
The hydrostatic part gives zero shear on every plane, so yield depends on the deviator

boards.prompt: Write radial equilibrium for an axisymmetric body in polar coordinates. Where does the extra term come from? Now spin the body.
points: dσ_rr/dr + (σ_rr − σ_θθ)/r + b_r = 0
The hoop stress on the two angled side faces has a radial resultant pointing inward
The outer face r dθ is larger than the inner face
Spinning adds the inertial term as a body force b_r = ρω²r
Lamé thick cylinders and spinning discs both start from this equation

boards.prompt: Pair each stress measure with its work conjugate strain rate. Why does it matter which pair you use?
points: σ pairs with D, power per unit current volume
P pairs with Ḟ, power per unit reference volume
S pairs with Ė, also per unit reference volume
Kirchhoff stress τ = Jσ pairs with D per unit reference volume
J σ:D = P:Ḟ = S:Ė, the same stress power
A hyperelastic law uses a conjugate pair: S = ∂W/∂E and P = ∂W/∂F

boards.prompt: Write isotropic Hooke's law in Lamé form and in E, ν form, and convert between the constants.
points: σ = λ tr(ε) I + 2με
ε = ((1 + ν)/E) σ − (ν/E) tr(σ) I

boards.prompt: What limits does a positive strain energy put on Poisson's ratio? What happens as ν approaches one half, and what is a material with negative ν?
points: Positive definite strain energy requires G > 0 and K > 0
With E > 0 that gives −1 < ν < 1/2
As ν → 1/2, K and λ tend to infinity, the incompressible limit
ν < 0 is auxetic: the material expands laterally in tension
Cork ν ≈ 0, metals ν ≈ 0.3, rubber ν ≈ 0.5

boards.prompt: A strain gauge rosette on a free surface reads ε_x, ε_y and γ_xy. Give me the stresses, and the through-thickness strain.
points: A free surface is in plane stress, σ_z = 0
σ_x = E(ε_x + νε_y)/(1 − ν²)
σ_y = E(ε_y + νε_x)/(1 − ν²)
τ_xy = Gγ_xy with G = E/(2(1 + ν))
ε_z = −ν(ε_x + ε_y)/(1 − ν), a nonzero through-thickness strain

boards.prompt: Compress a cylindrical sample inside a rigid frictionless sleeve. Find the axial stiffness and the lateral stress. Now let ν approach one half.
points: The sleeve holds the lateral strains at zero: ε₂₂ = ε₃₃ = 0
σ₁₁ = (λ + 2μ)ε₁₁, the constrained modulus M = λ + 2μ
M = E(1 − ν)/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)), stiffer than E
Lateral stress σ₂₂ = σ₃₃ = λε₁₁ = νσ₁₁/(1 − ν)
As ν → 1/2, M → ∞ and the lateral stress equals the axial stress, a hydrostatic state

boards.prompt: Write the stresses from an Airy function in polar coordinates. Solve the axisymmetric case, and tell me which term you throw away for a full ring.
points: σ_rr = (1/r)∂φ/∂r + (1/r²)∂²φ/∂θ²
σ_θθ = ∂²φ/∂r²
Axisymmetric φ = A ln r + B r² + C r² ln r + D
C r² ln r gives a multivalued hoop displacement in a full ring, so C = 0
σ_rr = A/r² + 2B and σ_θθ = −A/r² + 2B, the Lamé form

boards.prompt: You solved a traction problem with Airy in plane strain. Now the body is a thin plate in plane stress. What changes, the stresses or the displacements?
points: With zero body force, compatibility gives ∇⁴φ = 0 in both cases
For traction boundary conditions on a simply connected body the in-plane stresses are identical
Displacements change: replace E and ν by E/(1 − ν²) and ν/(1 − ν) to go from plane stress to plane strain
Plane strain carries σ₃₃ = ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂)
Plane stress carries ε₃₃ = −ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂)/E

boards.prompt: Add a body force to the Airy formulation, say gravity on a vertical plate or a dam. How do the definitions and the governing equation change?
points: Write a conservative body force as b = −∇V
σ₁₁ = ∂²φ/∂y² + V, σ₂₂ = ∂²φ/∂x² + V, σ₁₂ = −∂²φ/∂x∂y
These satisfy equilibrium with the body force identically
Compatibility in plane stress becomes ∇⁴φ = −(1 − ν)∇²V
Gravity b = −ρg e_y gives V = ρgy with ∇²V = 0, so ∇⁴φ = 0 still holds

boards.prompt: Use φ = a y³ on a beam of depth 2c loaded by end moments M. Show it gives the flexure formula, and tell me in what sense the answer is exact.
points: ∇⁴(a y³) = 0, so compatibility holds
σ₁₁ = 6a y, σ₂₂ = 0, σ₁₂ = 0
The top and bottom faces y = ±c are traction free
Matching the end moment fixes a and gives σ₁₁ = My/I in magnitude, linear through the depth
Exact when the end tractions are linear in y; for other end loading it holds a beam depth or so from the ends by Saint-Venant

boards.prompt: Derive the membrane stress in a thin spherical shell. Then weld a hemispherical cap onto a cylinder. What happens at the junction?
points: Hemisphere free body: σ 2πRt = pπR², so σ = pR/(2t) in every tangent direction
Cylinder: hoop pR/t, axial pR/(2t)
Free radial growth: cylinder (pR²/(2Et))(2 − ν), sphere (pR²/(2Et))(1 − ν)
The growth mismatch forces a shear force and a bending moment at the junction
The local bending stresses decay over a length of order √(Rt)

boards.prompt: Why does a boiled sausage split along its length? Now wind a pressure tank with helical fibres only. What winding angle do you pick?
points: Hoop stress pR/t is twice the axial stress pR/(2t)
The crack opens under the larger hoop stress, so it runs along the length
Netting analysis: the fibres carry all the load in tension
Hoop and axial balance give tan²α = 2, α ≈ 54.7° from the axis

boards.prompt: How much does the internal volume of a closed thin cylinder grow under pressure? When would you need that number?
points: ΔV/V = 2ε_θ + ε_x
It sets the extra fluid you pump in during a hydrostatic proof test

boards.prompt: A thin ring spins at angular speed ω. Find the hoop stress and the fastest it can spin.
points: Free body of a ring element: σA dθ = ρAR dθ ω²R
σ_θ = ρω²R² = ρv² with rim speed v = ωR
The stress is independent of the cross-section size
Burst rim speed v = √(σ_allow/ρ)
Specific strength σ/ρ sets the limit, so flywheel rims use carbon fibre

boards.prompt: Write the Mooney-Rivlin energy and show what it adds to neo-Hookean in uniaxial tension. How do you fit it from test data?
points: W = C₁(I₁ − 3) + C₂(I₂ − 3) for an incompressible solid
Neo-Hookean is the special case C₂ = 0
Small strain shear modulus μ = 2(C₁ + C₂)
Uniaxial nominal stress P = 2(λ − λ⁻²)(C₁ + C₂/λ)
Mooney plot: P/(2(λ − λ⁻²)) against 1/λ is a straight line with intercept C₁ and slope C₂

boards.prompt: Stretch a wide, short rubber strip so its width stays fixed. Neo-Hookean and incompressible. Find the stresses. Why is this test called pure shear?
points: λ₁ = λ, λ₂ = 1, λ₃ = 1/λ
σ = −pI + μB with B = diag(λ², 1, λ⁻²)
The traction-free faces give σ₃₃ = 0, so p = μλ⁻²
σ₁₁ = μ(λ² − λ⁻²), and σ₂₂ = μ(1 − λ⁻²) holds the width
The principal axes stay fixed and the 1-3 stretches are λ and 1/λ, a pure shear in that plane

boards.prompt: Why is rubber elasticity called entropic? What happens to the stiffness when you heat rubber, and what does a stretched band do when you heat it?
points: Stretching aligns the chains and lowers their configurational entropy
The retractive force comes from that entropy change
A Gaussian chain network gives neo-Hookean W = (μ/2)(I₁ − 3) with μ = nkT
The shear modulus grows in proportion to absolute temperature
A band held under load at moderate stretch contracts on heating, and it warms when stretched quickly

boards.prompt: A body is deformed twice in sequence. How do the deformation gradients combine? Use that to split thermal and elastic deformation, then elastic and plastic.
points: Successive deformations compose by multiplication, F = F₂F₁
Volume ratios multiply, J = J₂J₁
Isotropic thermal part F_θ = (1 + αΔT) I
The elastic part F_e = F F_θ⁻¹ produces the stress
Plasticity: F = F_e F_p with det F_p = 1, isochoric plastic flow

boards.prompt: Derive the local energy equation from the first law. Identify the stress power and write the referential form.
points: Rate of kinetic plus internal energy equals the power of external forces plus the heat supply
Local form ρė = σ:D − div q + ρr
Momentum balance cancels the kinetic energy terms, leaving the stress power σ:D
Referential form ρ₀ė = P:Ḟ − Div Q + ρ₀r
Fourier's law q = −k∇T closes the heat flux

boards.prompt: What does the entropy inequality tell you about an elastic material? Walk me through the argument.
points: Clausius-Duhem: ρη̇ ≥ ρr/T − div(q/T)
With the free energy ψ = e − Tη: σ:D − ρ(ψ̇ + ηṪ) − q·∇T/T ≥ 0
For ψ(E, T) the rates Ė and Ṫ are arbitrary, so S = ρ₀ ∂ψ/∂E and η = −∂ψ/∂T
The remaining inequality q·∇T ≤ 0: heat flows from hot to cold
So an elastic material is hyperelastic, its stress derives from a free energy (Coleman-Noll)

boards.prompt: Write linear momentum balance in referential form, linearize it for an isotropic solid, and give me the wave speeds.
points: Referential balance Div P + ρ₀b = ρ₀ü
Small strain isotropic gives Navier: μ∇²u + (λ + μ)∇(div u) + ρb = ρü
Longitudinal wave speed c_L = √((λ + 2μ)/ρ)
Shear wave speed c_T = √(μ/ρ)
c_L exceeds c_T, so the longitudinal wave arrives first
A thin bar carries waves at c = √(E/ρ)

boards.prompt: A bar hangs from the ceiling under its own weight. Integrate equilibrium for the stress and the elongation. How long can it get before it breaks?
points: Equilibrium dσ/dx = ρg with x measured up from the free end
σ(x) = ρgx, maximum ρgL at the support
Elongation δ = ρgL²/(2E), half that of the full weight hung at the end
Breaking length L = σ_f/(ρg), independent of the area
A uniform strength bar tapers its area as A₀ exp(ρgx/σ)

boards.prompt: Two strips with different expansion coefficients are bonded and heated. Which way does the strip curve, and what sets the curvature?
points: The layer with the higher α ends up on the convex side
Interface strain compatibility ties the two layers together
The axial forces in the layers are equal and opposite, and their couple bends the strip
Equal thickness and modulus: κ = 3(α₂ − α₁)ΔT/(2h), with h the total thickness
Thermostats and bimorph actuators use this effect

boards.prompt: A free plate has a temperature that varies through its thickness. Take a linear profile first, then a parabolic one. Where are the stresses?
points: A linear T(z) gives a compatible thermal strain: the plate bends with κ = αΔT/h and stays stress free
A parabolic T(z) gives a self-equilibrated residual stress
σ = −Eα(T − T_lin)/(1 − ν), with T_lin the linear part carrying the net force and moment
Regions hotter than T_lin are in compression
Biaxial restraint in the plane gives the factor 1/(1 − ν)

boards.prompt: Quench a hot ceramic plate in cold water. Where does it crack, and what material index resists thermal shock?
points: The surface cools first and wants to contract
The hot core holds it, so the surface goes into tension
A fully restrained surface sees σ = EαΔT/(1 − ν)
Brittle ceramics crack from the surface in tension
Resistance index ΔT_max = σ_f(1 − ν)/(Eα); high conductivity also helps

boards.prompt: Estimate the thermal expansion of a unidirectional carbon/epoxy lamina along the fibres. Why can a carbon structure have almost zero expansion?
points: Equal axial strain in fibre and matrix with zero net axial force
α₁ = (E_f α_f V_f + E_m α_m V_m)/(E_f V_f + E_m V_m)
The stiff fibres dominate α₁
Carbon fibre α_f is slightly negative, so α₁ is close to zero
α₂ across the fibres is matrix dominated and much larger
Layups tuned to near zero expansion hold telescope and antenna shapes
